figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematics of the network model. The model consists of a network of NE = 800 excitatory (triangles) and NI = 200 inhibitory (circles) neurons randomly connected via conductancebased synapses. The excitatory and inhibitory populations in the model interact via synaptic weights wEI (E → I) and wIE (I → E), characterized by synaptic delays dEIsyn and dIEsyn, respectively. Recurrent interactions within each populations are mediated by synaptic weights wEE (E → E) in the excitatory population and wII (I → I) in the inhibitory population, characterized by synaptic delays dEEsyn and dIIsyn, respectively.
Table 1: Parameters of the network and neuron model used in our simulations.

Figure 2: Dynamics of the excitatory-inhibitory network model. (A) Raster plot (top) and corresponding population activity (bottom) of the network of excitatory (blue) and inhibitory (red) neurons, exhibiting self-sustained oscillations characteristic of the PING mechanism. Model parameters are given in Table 1, with dsyn = 2.5ms. The level of synchrony (assessed by calculating pFF) is indicated above the panel (pFF = 2.62). (B) Spike count irregularity of individual neurons (assessed by calculating CV). (C) PSD of the population activity, showing a prominent oscillatory peak at approximately 50 Hz.

Figure 3: Delay-dependent changes in oscillation frequency and synchrony. (A) The peak frequency of the PSD as a function of synaptic delays. (B) The level of synchrony (assessed by calculating pFF) for different synaptic delays. (C1, C2) Representative raster plot (top) and corresponding population activity (bottom) of the network for dsyn = 3.0ms (C1) and dsyn = 5.0ms (C2). pFF is indicated above each panel with pFF = 4.61 for panel C1 and pFF = 6.92 for panel C2.

Figure 4: Phase and amplitude responses to external stimulation of the excitatory population. The nPRC (A) and nARC (B) of the excitatory-inhibitory network obtained by perturbing the excitatory population with different synaptic delays in synchronized state (see Methods). The gray dashed lines indicate zero response.

Figure 5: Representative response of the excitatory-inhibitory network to excitatory population perturbation. Raster plots (A1, B1) and population activity (A2, B2) responses following a brief excitatory pulse applied to the excitatory population at a selected phase of the oscillation cycle for a shorter synaptic delay (dsyn = 2.5 ms), and a longer synaptic delay (dsyn = 5.0 ms). Raster plots show excitatory (blue) and inhibitory (red) neuronal activity before (baseline) and after the perturbation (red dashed line indicates the pulse timing). Population activity traces before (gray) and after (green) perturbation show the phase shift and amplitude modulation of subsequent oscillatory cycles. The perturbed oscillation peaks are indicated by red markers. The results demonstrate that excitatory stimulation can advance population rhythms and enhance oscillation amplitude through transient recruitment of excitatory neurons within the PING feedback loop.

Figure 6: Phase and amplitude responses to external stimulation of the inhibitory population. The nPRC (A) and nARC (B) of the excitatory-inhibitory network obtained by perturbing the inhibitory population with different synaptic delays in synchronized state. The gray dashed lines indicate zero response.

Figure 7: Phase and amplitude responses to external stimulation of the whole excitatoryinhibitory network. The nPRC (A) and nARC (B) of the excitatory-inhibitory network obtained by perturbing the whole network with different synaptic delays in synchronized state. The gray dashed line indicates zero response.

Figure 8: Summary of delay-dependent changes in population phase and amplitude modulations. Extrema of the nPRC (top row; A1-C1) and nARC (bottom row; A2-C2) for θ > 0.5 as a function of synaptic delay for excitatory (left column; A1 and A2), inhibitory (middle column; B1 and B2), and whole-network (right column; C1 and C2) stimulation. The maximum and minimum response values quantify how synaptic delays regulate the strength and polarity of perturbation-induced changes in population oscillations. The gray dashed lines indicate zero response. This summary highlights synaptic delay as a key parameter controlling the phase sensitivity and amplitude stability of collective oscillations in excitatory-inhibitory networks.
